title: Ring fit by region clustering: e-means over face labels seeded from the ring regions, keeping each region's topology

description:
Follow-on to the e-means port (CRAW-111): fit the rings by clustering the surface's faces into regions that keep the topology the rings were drawn with. The unknowns are face labels, not ring anchors; rings are read off at the end as the boundaries between labels. Compare against the ring anchor fit (CRAW-106) on its own fixtures.

## The model

1. Iteration 0: RingRegions floods the faces between the rings and bisectors as drawn. Each region is one cluster; k is the region count after sliver regions are merged, and never changes. Each region keeps its index, so each drawn ring maps to the pair of regions it separates (boundingRingsByRegion).
2. Each region has a centroid: a face inside the region (the one minimising area-weighted geodesic distance to the region's faces), never a point in space.
3. A face's cost for a label is its geodesic distance to that label's centroid, with crossing groove-like surface made expensive, so a boundary is cheap to sit in a groove and otherwise settles halfway between centroids.
4. Each pass takes a mini-batch of boundary faces; each switches to the cheaper label it touches, subject to the topology rule. Centroids move by the e-means update (moving-average count and sum per region, step shrinking along a cosine to a tenth), using the port from CRAW-111.
5. Repeat until no face switches. Each drawn ring is replaced by the boundary between its two regions; rings keep their labels.

## The topology rule

A face may switch from region a to region b only if:
1. it shares an edge with a b face;
2. among the faces around it, the a faces form one connected run, and so do the b faces (the simple-point test from digital topology, as in topology-preserving level sets, Han, Xu, Prince 2003);
3. it is not a's last face.

So a region cannot split, gain a hole or vanish; rings cannot split, merge, cross, overlap or disappear. Every face has one label, so two boundaries can only meet where three labels meet (bisector ends).

## Why this should pass the CRAW-106 cases without a "groove no other ring holds" term

On the one-groove, two-ring torus (ofTwoRingsOnATorusWithOneGrooveOneTakesItAndTheOtherStandsOpposite), the two rings make two regions. At equilibrium each boundary is halfway between the two centroids along its arc, so the two boundaries are always 180 degrees apart; the groove cost picks the rotation. Both cannot take the groove because that empties a region, which the rule forbids.

## Charts

A UV atlas with tracked seam transitions (as the quad layout pipeline uses) is an acceptable space for distances and centroids if it is simpler than geodesic distance on the mesh; the groove cost is needed either way.

## Rings that split nothing

A ring with the same region on both sides of every edge, with all rings in place (RingRegions.ringSplitsNothing, a lone loop round a handle), is no boundary between labels, so the clustering cannot move it: it stays where it was drawn (decided by the user).

## Results (RegionClusterFit, pull weight 2)

RingFitBench.run over the 17 CRAW-113 cases: **9 pass**, against 3 for the CRAW-106 fit_ring_anchors baseline.

| case | clustering | CRAW-106 baseline |
|---|---|---|
| one_groove | pass | pass |
| one_groove_crease | pass | fail |
| one_groove_far | pass | pass |
| two_grooves_nearer_second | pass | fail |
| two_grooves_nearer_first | pass | fail |
| two_grooves_crease | pass | fail |
| two_grooves_two_rings_near_one | pass | fail |
| two_grooves_two_rings_each_own | pass | pass |
| one_groove_two_rings | pass (ring_01 within 9 deg of opposite) | fail |
| two_grooves_one_ring_nearest_both | fail: 6.75 / 124.5 deg | fail |
| slanted_ring | fail: 12.75 deg | fail |
| slanted_ring_trenches | fail: 10.5 deg, misses the +15 deg groove | fail |
| tree_partly_in_groove | fail: 3.63 deg | fail |
| bisector_grooved_rings | fail: 81 deg (bisector rings are held fixed) | fail |
| bisector_smooth_rings | fail: 72 deg (bisector rings are held fixed) | fail |
| horn cases | fail: 1.11 and 1.14 from the foot, tolerance 0.08 | fail |

Pull weight sweep: at 0.5 also 9 pass, but one_groove_two_rings' second ring ends 4.49 deg off. At 32, 8 pass: two_grooves_one_ring_nearest_both's ring_00 is fixed, but one_groove_two_rings' second ring ends 22.5 deg off, and the horns end about 0.85 off. Balance against pull is the trade-off; the horns, whose parts are meant to be unequal, conflict with area balance itself.

## Deviations from the model above

1. Moves are whole strips, not single faces: each ring is an edge loop and a move shifts it by the fan of faces on one side. The topology rule is checked on the new loop (one simple cycle, not on the border, touching no other ring, not emptying a region) instead of the per-face simple-point test. Same guarantees, far fewer moves.
2. An added groove pull term: edge length times distance to the nearest groove bottom, normalised by mean edge squared, weighted by the pull weight. Balance alone settles rings halfway between centroids and does not reach grooves strongly enough.
3. Rings that split nothing feel the pull only (the hidden ring glued to the real one, as the user agreed), so they slide into grooves instead of staying as drawn.
4. Bisectors (open rings) and the closed rings they attach to stay fixed: the bisector cases fail for that reason.

## Resolved unknowns

- Groove cost units: dimensionless weights. Crossing weight multiplies a face distance by (1 + weight x crease strength); pull weight scales the groove-distance term relative to the balance term.
- Distance: geodesic over the face graph (Dijkstra on face adjacency), no UV atlas.

## Constants for the user to decide

- Pull weight (DEFAULT_PULL_WEIGHT) = 2.0
- Crossing weight (DEFAULT_CROSSING_WEIGHT) = 1.0
- Batch faces for the e-means mean update (DEFAULT_BATCH_FACES) = 1024
- E-means step alpha0 (DEFAULT_ALPHA0) = 0.5, cosine schedule to a tenth (EMeans.scheduledStep)
- Max passes (DEFAULT_MAX_PASSES) = 400; stop after STALL_PASSES = 5 passes without a move
- Groove bottom: crease strength >= SurfaceCreases.CREASE_STRENGTH (0.5) and curvature within BOTTOM_TIE = 1e-3 of every neighbour's maximum
- Seed (DEFAULT_SEED) = 1234

## Note: cross-field cones as seeds

The cross field's cones (singularities) may be good seeds for ring segmentation: they often sit at saddles and extrema, which is where part boundaries and part tips are. Worth checking whether seeding regions, or ring candidates, from the cones beats seeding from hand-drawn rings alone. (User note, 2026-11-22, from the T-Rex skull work in CRAW-114.)
definition-of-done:
1. The region clustering above, built on the CRAW-111 e-means port, with the topology rule enforced on every switch.
2. A unit test of the topology rule: a switch that would split a region, open a hole or empty a region is refused.
3. Every CRAW-113 ring-fit bench case run through the clustering with RingFitBench.run, with a table on this ticket: which cases pass and how far each ring ends from its expected place, compared with the CRAW-106 fit_ring_anchors baseline recorded on CRAW-113.
4. The bench's one_groove_two_rings case passes: one ring in the groove, the other within the bench's OPPOSITE tolerance of 180 degrees.
5. A ring-scene look showing the regions and boundaries per pass, a launch.json entry, and before/after screenshots under tmp/.
6. Every constant (groove crossing cost, batch size, step) listed on this ticket for the user to decide.
testing-plan: 1. Topology rule unit test (split, hole, empty region refused). 2. The RingAnchorFitTest fixtures, run through the clustering. 3. The one-groove two-ring torus: one ring in the groove, the other opposite.
todos: Classify and log every further fit attempt in ai-workspace ring_fit_failed_approaches.md before reporting it: first check whether it is an existing entry (F1-F13) under a new name, and if so add the name to that entry's 'Also called' line and record the run under it; otherwise add the next F entry with every name it went by, what it does, where it was tried and its bench count, and why it failed (measured, or in the user's words). Do not propose an approach already listed without saying which entry it is and what is new.
changes-made: RegionClusterFit: rings move as edge loops by whole face strips, energy = region balance (e-means centroids, groove-stretched face distance) + pull weight x distance to groove bottoms; topology rule on every new loop
EMeans.scheduledStep extracted so the fit shares the cosine step schedule
RingScene: cluster-fit look (Y steps a pass, shift+Y back) showing regions and rings per pass
RegionClusterFitTest: topology refusals (merge, hole, pinch, empty horn), one_groove_two_rings passes, at least 9 of 17 bench cases pass

2026-11-15: wrote ai-workspace ring_fit_failed_approaches.md, a catalogue of the ring-fit approaches that have failed in craw-106 and craw-112 (F1-F13), the user's requirements they break, and the names each has gone by. The heat-field descent with taken-groove exclusion (F12) scored 13 of 18 on the bench, uncommitted in craw-112.
review-summary: Adds RegionClusterFit, which fits drawn rings by balancing the face regions between them while pulling each ring toward a groove, never letting a region split, merge or vanish. It replaces the per-anchor groove search that missed most bench cases.
